rules.name: Environment file access
rules.description: Skill attempts to read .env, credentials, or secret files
rules.remediation: Do not read .env files, credentials, or secret files directly. Use environment variables passed by the agent runtime. If the skill needs API keys, declare them as required configuration parameters — never read them from the filesystem.

rules.name: Credential reference (documentation)
rules.description: Skill references API keys in setup/config context — likely safe
rules.remediation: This is likely documentation showing how to configure credentials. No action needed if in a setup guide. If this is executable code, use environment variables instead of hardcoding.

rules.name: Data exfiltration attempt
rules.description: Skill sends data to known exfiltration endpoints
rules.remediation: Remove all references to known exfiltration endpoints (webhook.site, requestbin, ngrok, etc.). If the skill needs to send data externally, use well-known, reputable services and document the data flow clearly.

rules.name: Suspicious outbound data transfer
rules.description: Skill reads sensitive files and POSTs data externally
rules.remediation: Do not read files and POST their contents externally in the same flow. If the skill legitimately needs to upload files, use documented APIs with explicit user consent and avoid piping sensitive file contents to curl/wget.

rules.name: Prompt injection attempt
rules.description: Skill contains instructions that override agent behavior
rules.remediation: Remove any instructions that override agent behavior ("ignore previous instructions", "you are now", etc.). Skill descriptions should describe what the tool does, not instruct the agent on how to behave.

rules.name: Shell command execution
rules.description: Skill executes shell commands that could be dangerous
rules.remediation: Avoid using eval(), exec(), spawn(), or child_process with dynamic input. Use parameterized APIs instead of shell commands. If shell execution is necessary, validate and sanitize all inputs, use allowlists, and never pass user input directly. NOTE: ``child_process`` and ``execSync`` patterns now use ``\b`` word boundaries so they no longer match inside longer identifiers (`CHILD_PROCESS_EXEC` enum members, `my_execSync_wrapper` etc.). Real Node.js usage `child_process.exec(...)` / `execSync(cmd)` is still matched. The always-shell string-sink pattern (``os.popen`` / ``subprocess.get[status]output`` / ``commands.get[status]output`` / ``asyncio.create_subprocess_shell``) matches the bare CALL form so the Python context classifier (``_skillaudit_python_context._classify_call``) is consulted: a reassembled / variable / concat argument stays SUSPECT (kept), while a pure-literal argument (``os.popen('ls')``) is proven inert and suppressed. The trailing ``\s*\(`` requires an actual call (no FP on identifiers like ``getoutputs`` / ``my_os.popener``); ``os.system`` and ``pty.spawn`` already match the patterns above, and the argv-form ``asyncio.create_subprocess_exec`` is deliberately excluded because it bypasses the shell.

rules.name: Suspicious network activity
rules.description: Skill makes network requests to unusual destinations
rules.remediation: Do not use raw IP addresses for network requests. Use proper domain names with HTTPS. Avoid encoding URLs in base64 or using obfuscation techniques for network endpoints.

rules.name: Filesystem write operations
rules.description: Skill writes to potentially sensitive locations
rules.remediation: Do not write to system directories (/etc/, /usr/, /bin/) or user dotfiles (.bashrc, .profile, .zshrc). Write only to designated output directories. Never modify crontab or system configuration files. NOTE: dotfile patterns now require a path-like prefix (start-of-line, `/`, `~`, whitespace, or quote) so method calls like ``xai.profile()`` / ``api.profile()`` / ``user.profile_url`` don't match — only ``~/.profile``, ``/etc/.bashrc``, ``"~/.zshrc"`` and similar real path references do.

rules.name: Code obfuscation detected
rules.description: Skill contains obfuscated or encoded payloads
rules.remediation: Remove all code obfuscation (hex escapes, String.fromCharCode, base64-encoded payloads, unescape). Legitimate skills have no reason to obfuscate their code. Write clear, readable code that can be audited.

rules.name: Privilege escalation attempt
rules.description: Skill attempts to gain elevated permissions
rules.remediation: Remove all privilege escalation attempts (sudo, pkexec, doas, chmod +s, setuid, chown root). Skills should operate with minimal permissions. If elevated access is needed, document it as a requirement and let the user grant it explicitly.

rules.name: Cryptocurrency wallet theft
rules.description: Skill attempts to access crypto wallets or seed phrases
rules.remediation: Do not access cryptocurrency wallets, seed phrases, mnemonics, or private keys. If the skill works with crypto, use secure APIs and never handle raw key material directly.

rules.name: Token/cookie stealing
rules.description: Skill attempts to steal auth tokens, cookies, or session data
rules.remediation: Do not access cookies, localStorage tokens, session storage, or browser credentials. If auth is needed, use the agent runtime's built-in authentication mechanisms rather than stealing tokens from the environment.

rules.name: DNS rebinding attempt
rules.description: Skill uses DNS rebinding techniques to access internal services
rules.remediation: Remove DNS rebinding patterns and references to rebinding services (nip.io, rbndr.us). Use proper domain names for all network requests and validate hostnames server-side.

rules.name: Reverse shell
rules.description: Skill attempts to establish a reverse shell connection
rules.remediation: Remove all reverse shell code immediately. There is no legitimate reason for a skill to establish a reverse shell connection. This is a critical indicator of malicious intent.

rules.name: Agent memory/config modification
rules.description: Skill attempts to modify agent memory, soul, or config files
rules.remediation: Do not modify agent memory, soul, or configuration files (MEMORY.md, SOUL.md, AGENTS.md). Skills should only output results through their declared interface, never modify the agent's core files.

rules.name: Tool output poisoning
rules.description: Skill injects hidden instructions in tool output to manipulate the calling agent's behavior
rules.remediation: Remove all hidden instructions in tool output ([INST], <<SYS>>, IMPORTANT:, NOTE TO AI:). Tool output should contain only the result of the tool's operation, never instructions for the agent.

rules.name: Tool shadowing / redefinition
rules.description: Skill attempts to redefine, override, or shadow other tools to intercept their data
rules.remediation: Do not override, redefine, or proxy other tools. Each skill should operate independently within its declared scope. Remove all monkey-patching, prototype modification, and tool interception code. NOTE: the override/redefine/replace/intercept/proxy patterns now use bounded `.{0,N}` spans (was greedy `.*`) so they no longer match prose like `the scripts handle correctly but which you should not override if the user asks ... esptool ...` where `override` and `tool` are 50+ tokens apart in different clauses.

rules.name: Invisible Unicode / zero-width characters
rules.description: Skill contains invisible Unicode characters that may hide malicious instructions from human review
rules.remediation: Remove all invisible Unicode characters (zero-width spaces, joiners, directional overrides). These can hide malicious instructions from human reviewers. Use only visible, standard characters.

rules.name: Time-based activation / logic bomb
rules.description: Skill contains code that activates conditionally based on date, time, or execution count — may evade initial scanning
rules.remediation: Remove all time-based activation logic (date checks, delayed execution, dormant periods). Legitimate skills should function consistently regardless of when they're run. If scheduling is needed, use the agent's built-in scheduling capabilities. NOTE: pattern 5 now requires a LITERAL TIME DELTA (`\d+ days?`, `\d+ hours?`, `\d+ minutes?`) and bounded `.{0,40}` spans, so it no longer matches rate-limiter bash code that uses identifier names like `current_minute` and `last_minute` with no actual numeric delta — those are per-minute rate-limit windows, not time bombs.

rules.name: Server-Side Request Forgery (SSRF)
rules.description: Skill crafts requests to internal/cloud metadata endpoints or uses URL schemes to access internal services
rules.remediation: Do not make requests to internal/cloud metadata endpoints (169.254.169.254). Validate all URLs against an allowlist of expected domains. Never use file://, gopher://, or dict:// URL schemes. NOTE: http://localhost and http://127.0.0.1 are NOT in this rule — those are dev/example URLs that legitimately appear in MCP server docs, Wrangler dev examples, and test fixtures. Real SSRF concerns are cloud metadata endpoints and exotic URL schemes.

rules.name: Supply chain attack indicators
rules.description: Skill dynamically loads code from external sources or uses dependency confusion patterns
rules.remediation: Do not dynamically load code from external URLs (require("https://..."), eval(fetch(...))). Pin all dependencies to specific versions. Never pipe curl/wget output to a shell interpreter. NOTE: well-known CDN host exclusions (cdn.jsdelivr.net / unpkg.com / esm.sh / etc.) are handled in the markdown classifier (not in the regex itself, to preserve RE2 compatibility — RE2 disallows negative lookahead). Pinned ESM imports from those known CDNs get suppressed at classifier-time.

rules.name: Covert data exfiltration channel
rules.description: Skill uses DNS, image URLs, or other covert channels to exfiltrate data without obvious network calls
rules.remediation: Remove all covert data exfiltration channels (DNS tunneling, image beacons, navigator.sendBeacon with encoded data). If data needs to be sent externally, use documented, visible API calls with user consent.

rules.name: MCP schema poisoning
rules.description: Tool description or schema contains hidden instructions that manipulate the calling agent — a form of indirect prompt injection via the tool manifest itself
rules.remediation: Tool descriptions must only describe what the tool does. Remove all hidden instructions ("ignore previous", "secretly send", "do not tell the user"). Schema descriptions should be factual, not manipulative. NOTE: patterns now use bounded `.{0,N}` spans instead of greedy `.*` to prevent FPs on long legitimate descriptions that happen to contain a sneaky-adverb and an unrelated action verb within the same paragraph; and `without` was removed from the sneaky-adverb set because it is neutral (`without re-flashing, tail device logs` is benign). NOTE (issue #178): the first pattern additionally requires an OBJECT NOUN after the determiner (`previous|prior|other`) and word-boundary-anchors both ends. `previous`/`prior`/`other` are ordinary English determiners, so the bare form matched benign prose such as `... ignored maintenance mode ... had no effect on the other daemon ...`; and the unanchored determiner matched INSIDE a word (`an-other` in `overrides ... to impersonate another agent`). A poison directive must name what the agent should ignore, so requiring the object noun is FN-safe for this rule's threat class: measured across the whole plugin corpus the narrowing loses only the catalog's own self-referential text and the two FP shapes above, and keeps every genuine `ignore previous instructions` / `ignore other tools instructions` match. Up to 3 intervening modifier words are allowed (`ignore all previous user-supplied instructions`).

rules.name: Environment fingerprinting / reconnaissance
rules.description: Skill probes the host system to gather information about the environment — common precursor to targeted attacks
rules.remediation: Do not fingerprint the host environment (hostname, network interfaces, OS info, user info). If system information is needed for functionality, declare it as a required capability and document why.

rules.name: Persistence mechanism
rules.description: Skill installs persistence mechanisms to survive restarts — cron jobs, startup scripts, launch agents, or auto-run entries
rules.remediation: Remove all persistence mechanisms (crontab entries, systemctl enable, LaunchAgents, Registry Run keys, pm2 startup). Skills should execute on demand and terminate cleanly. They must never install themselves to run at startup.

rules.name: Cross-tool data access
rules.description: Skill attempts to access data or state belonging to other tools, or reads agent conversation history to extract sensitive information
rules.remediation: Do not access other tools' data, conversation history, or system prompts. Each skill should operate within its own declared scope. Use only the inputs provided through the tool's declared parameters.

rules.name: Container/sandbox escape attempt
rules.description: Skill attempts to escape container or sandbox isolation — accessing Docker socket, mounting host filesystem, or exploiting kernel interfaces
rules.remediation: Remove all container escape attempts (Docker socket access, nsenter, /proc/1/root, mount --bind, LD_PRELOAD). Skills must respect sandbox boundaries. If elevated access is needed, document it as a requirement. NOTE: ``mount.*(?:-o|--bind)`` was tightened to ``\bmount\s+(?:-[a-z]+\s+)*(?:-o|--bind|...)`` so it requires the `-o`/`--bind` flag to be an argv element of an actual `mount` command — not just `mount` appearing anywhere in prose followed by `-o` further along (the original greedy `.*` matched `flush-mounted ... no-ops` in the m5-onboard ESP32 hardware docs). Same tightening for ``docker exec/run/cp`` and ``capsh --print`` to require an actual command invocation, not prose mentioning the words separately.

rules.name: A2A agent impersonation / card spoofing
rules.description: Skill fabricates or overrides Agent Card metadata to impersonate another agent, claim false capabilities, or inject hidden instructions into the A2A discovery layer
rules.remediation: Do not spoof, forge, or clone Agent Card identities. Each agent must use its own authentic identity. Remove any code that fabricates agent IDs or claims false trusted status.

rules.name: A2A task hijacking / redirection
rules.description: Skill intercepts, redirects, or modifies tasks intended for other agents — hijacking the A2A task delegation flow
rules.remediation: Do not intercept, redirect, or modify tasks intended for other agents. Each agent should only process tasks explicitly delegated to it. Remove all MITM and task interception code.

rules.name: Cross-agent prompt injection via A2A
rules.description: Skill injects instructions or manipulative content into messages sent between agents through A2A protocol, poisoning the inter-agent communication channel
rules.remediation: Do not inject instructions into A2A messages. Inter-agent communications should contain only task-relevant data, never hidden prompts or commands for downstream agents.

rules.name: A2A inter-agent data leakage
rules.description: Skill exfiltrates data by embedding sensitive information in A2A task artifacts, messages, or metadata sent to external agents
rules.remediation: Do not embed sensitive data in A2A artifacts or metadata. Use encrypted, authenticated channels for sensitive data exchange. Never include credentials, env vars, or conversation history in inter-agent messages.

rules.name: A2A capability escalation / abuse
rules.description: Skill exploits A2A protocol to access capabilities beyond its declared scope — requesting elevated permissions, spawning unauthorized sub-agents, or chaining agent calls to bypass restrictions
rules.remediation: Do not escalate permissions or spawn unauthorized agents via A2A protocol. Operate within declared capabilities. Never self-register as trusted/admin or chain agent calls to bypass restrictions.

rules.name: Path traversal attack
rules.description: Skill uses directory traversal sequences to access files outside intended scope — reading /etc/passwd, escaping chroot, or navigating to sensitive system paths
rules.remediation: Validate and sanitize all file paths. Use path.resolve() and verify the resolved path is within the expected directory. Never pass user input directly to file operations. Block ../ sequences.

rules.name: Command injection
rules.description: Skill constructs shell commands from dynamic input using dangerous concatenation or template patterns — enables arbitrary command execution via ; | && `` $() injection
rules.remediation: Never construct shell commands from dynamic input using string concatenation or template literals. Use parameterized APIs (e.g., execFile instead of exec, subprocess.run with array args instead of shell=True). Validate all inputs against strict allowlists. NOTE: the `$(...)` and backtick patterns now require a NON-empty argument after the binary name (was: bare-binary alone matched). This eliminates the Claude Code hook stdin idiom `input=$(cat)` FP, and bare markdown inline-code teaching tool names `\`curl\`` / `\`ls\``. The pipe/semicolon `(?:;|\||&&)\s*\b(bash|...)` pattern stays intact for real shell metachar use, with markdown-table-cell FP handled in the markdown context classifier.

rules.name: Prototype pollution
rules.description: Skill manipulates JavaScript object prototypes to inject properties into all objects — enables privilege escalation, RCE, or denial of service across the entire runtime
rules.remediation: Do not merge untrusted input into objects without filtering __proto__ and constructor keys. Use Object.create(null) for lookup objects. Freeze prototypes with Object.freeze(Object.prototype). Validate all keys before assignment. NOTE: issue #131 (2026-06-17) — pattern 6 (the merge-family gadget shape) word-bounds the generic user-input identifiers (`\binput\b`/`\bpayload\b`/`\bparams\b`) so the canonical shadcn `cn(...inputs)`/`cn(...args)` helper `twMerge(clsx(inputs))` no longer matches on the `inputs`/`args` rest param, and broadens the explicit user-controlled identifier set (`userInput`/`user_input`/`req.body`/…). It deliberately does NOT word-bound the merge-family VERB: the scanner matches case-insensitively, so a leading `\b` would silently MISS real camelCase merge sinks (`recursiveMerge(req.body)`, lodash `mergeWith(req.query)`, `customMerge(userInput)`) — the ARGUMENT discriminator is what clears the benign Tailwind idiom, not a verb boundary. The verb alternation also enumerates the lodash/immutable deep-merge family (`mergeWith`/`mergeDeep`/`defaultsDeep`) so a `merge<Suffix>(` recursive-merge sink — which the verb-then-`(` anchor never caught — is now detected; benign `mergeSort(...)` is deliberately NOT in the list so it stays clear. The real proto-pollution sinks are still caught by patterns 1-5,7,8 (`__proto__[x]=`, `a["constructor"]["prototype"]=`, `Object.assign(target, JSON.parse(userInput))`, `Reflect.set(obj,"__proto__",…)`).

rules.name: Advanced SSRF / request smuggling
rules.description: Skill uses advanced SSRF techniques including URL parser differentials, IPv6 bypasses, or cloud metadata access via alternate encodings
rules.remediation: Validate all user-supplied URLs against a strict allowlist of domains. Block internal IP ranges (10.x, 172.16-31.x, 192.168.x, 127.x). Parse URLs server-side and reject schemes other than https://. Disable automatic redirects. NOTE: r05 ananddtyagi FP iter1 (2026-05-27) — patterns 1, 4, 8 now require user-input identifiers to be word-bounded (`\binput\b`, `\bparam\b`, `\bquery\b`) or to be standard camelCase/snake_case user-input var names (`userInput`, `userId`, `user_input`); bare `user` was too generic and fired on `fetch('/api/users')` and `HTMLInputElement`. `\brequest\(` no longer matches inside `handleRequest(` or `process_user_request(` function definitions. `req` requires a property access shape (`req.url`, `req.body`).

rules.name: ReDoS / catastrophic regex
rules.description: Skill contains regex patterns with nested quantifiers that can cause catastrophic backtracking — enabling denial of service via specially crafted input strings
rules.remediation: Never construct RegExp from user input without sanitization. Avoid nested quantifiers (e.g., (a+)+). Use regex timeout libraries. Test patterns with worst-case inputs. Consider using RE2 for untrusted patterns.

rules.name: Unsafe deserialization
rules.description: Skill deserializes untrusted data using formats that allow arbitrary code execution — pickle, yaml.unsafe_load, Java ObjectInputStream, PHP unserialize, or Ruby Marshal with user input
rules.remediation: Never deserialize untrusted data with pickle, yaml.unsafe_load, or Java ObjectInputStream. Use safe alternatives: json.loads(), yaml.safe_load()/SafeLoader, torch.load(weights_only=True). Validate data format before processing.

rules.name: Server-Side Template Injection (SSTI)
rules.description: Skill renders templates with user-controlled input without sandboxing — enables arbitrary code execution via template engines like Jinja2, Mako, ERB, Pug, or Handlebars
rules.remediation: Never pass user input to template constructors (Template(), render_template_string()). Use pre-compiled templates with auto-escaping enabled. Sandbox template engines. Use Jinja2 with SandboxedEnvironment. NOTE: pattern 1 now requires NO space between Template/Environment and the opening paren — English prose like `- Environment (required vars, setup)` no longer matches.

rules.name: XML External Entity (XXE) injection
rules.description: Skill parses XML with external entity processing enabled — allows reading arbitrary files, SSRF via file:// and http:// URIs, and denial of service via recursive entity expansion (billion laughs attack)
rules.remediation: Disable external entity processing in all XML parsers. Set resolve_entities=False in lxml, use defusedxml in Python, set FEATURE_EXTERNAL_GENERAL_ENTITIES to false in Java. Never parse XML from untrusted sources without these protections.

rules.name: Wallet drainer / token approval exploit
rules.description: Skill performs unlimited token approvals, suspicious transfers, or drains wallet balances via smart contract calls — common in crypto-targeted agent attacks
rules.remediation: Never approve unlimited token spending (MAX_UINT256). Use exact amount approvals and revoke after use. Validate all transaction recipients. Never sign transactions without explicit user confirmation and amount display.

rules.name: Environment variable injection / poisoning
rules.description: Skill modifies environment variables to poison other processes, hijack library loading, alter PATH, or inject credentials into the runtime — differs from env reading (reconnaissance) by actively modifying the environment
rules.remediation: Do not modify environment variables programmatically. Never set PATH, LD_PRELOAD, NODE_OPTIONS, or credential env vars. If configuration is needed, use config files with proper access controls instead of environment manipulation. NOTE: removed the AWS_/OPENAI_/ANTHROPIC_/GOOGLE_/AZURE_/DATABASE_/DB_/REDIS_/MONGO_ prefix pattern because those are not language-runtime-hijack vars — setting `export DATABASE_URL=...` in install docs is routine configuration, not persistence. The remaining LD_PRELOAD/NODE_OPTIONS/PYTHONPATH/PYTHONSTARTUP/PERL5LIB/RUBYLIB/CLASSPATH/PATH patterns ARE real hijack vectors and stay.

rules.name: Log injection / log4shell / JNDI exploitation
rules.description: Skill injects malicious payloads into log output — exploiting log4j JNDI lookups, LDAP injection, or crafting log entries that trigger code execution in vulnerable logging frameworks
rules.remediation: Sanitize all user input before logging — strip JNDI lookup strings, newlines, and control characters. Update log4j to 2.17.1+. Set log4j2.formatMsgNoLookups=true. Never log raw request data without sanitization.

rules.name: JWT security vulnerability
rules.description: Skill contains insecure JWT handling — algorithm confusion attacks, missing verification, hardcoded tokens, or disabled signature validation can lead to authentication bypass and privilege escalation
rules.remediation: Always verify JWT signatures before trusting claims. Never allow algorithm "none". Use RS256 or ES256 with proper key management — avoid HS256 with short or hardcoded secrets. Set and validate expiration (exp) and not-before (nbf) claims. Never decode JWTs without verification in production code. Remove any hardcoded JWT tokens from source.

rules.name: Insecure cryptographic practice
rules.description: Skill uses broken or weak cryptographic primitives — MD5/SHA1 for security purposes, Math.random() for tokens, weak key sizes, or insecure cipher modes that can be exploited to forge data, predict tokens, or decrypt communications
rules.remediation: Use SHA-256 or SHA-3 instead of MD5/SHA1 for any security purpose. Use crypto.randomBytes() or secrets.token_hex() instead of Math.random()/random.random() for tokens, keys, or security-sensitive values. Use AES-GCM or ChaCha20-Poly1305 instead of ECB, DES, RC4, or Blowfish. Use minimum 2048-bit RSA or 256-bit ECC keys. Never hardcode encryption keys in source.

rules.name: SQL injection vulnerability
rules.description: Skill constructs SQL queries using string concatenation or template literals with user input — allows attackers to read, modify, or delete database contents, bypass authentication, or execute OS commands via xp_cmdshell/LOAD_FILE
rules.remediation: NEVER construct SQL queries with string concatenation, template literals, or f-strings using user input. Use parameterized queries (prepared statements) in every case: Node.js db.query('SELECT * FROM users WHERE id = $1', [userId]); Python cursor.execute('SELECT * FROM users WHERE id = %s', (user_id,)); Java PreparedStatement with setString(). Use an ORM (Sequelize, SQLAlchemy, Prisma) which parameterizes by default. If raw queries are unavoidable, use the ORM's parameterized raw query method.

rules.name: Cross-site scripting (XSS) vulnerability
rules.description: Skill inserts user-controlled input into HTML output without sanitization — allows attackers to execute JavaScript in victims' browsers, steal cookies/sessions, redirect users, or deface pages
rules.remediation: Never insert user input directly into HTML. Use textContent instead of innerHTML for text. Use template engines with auto-escaping enabled (Jinja2 with autoescape=True, React JSX which escapes by default, Handlebars {{}} double-curly which escapes). If HTML is necessary, sanitize with DOMPurify (client-side) or sanitize-html (server-side). Set Content-Security-Policy headers. Use HttpOnly and Secure flags on cookies. In React, avoid dangerouslySetInnerHTML with user data. In Vue, avoid v-html with user data.

rules.name: Indirect prompt injection via tool output
rules.description: Content contains hidden instructions designed to be returned to an AI agent via tool output — the attacker embeds commands in data the agent will read (web pages, files, API responses) to hijack the agent's behavior without the user noticing
rules.remediation: If you're a skill author: never embed hidden instructions in tool output, web content, or data files. If you're an agent developer: treat ALL tool output as untrusted user data — never execute instructions found in tool results. Implement output filtering that strips instruction-like content from tool responses. Use structured output (JSON) rather than free text for tool results. Deploy an 'instruction hierarchy' where system prompts always override content found in data.

rules.name: Tool use confusion attack
rules.description: Content attempts to confuse an AI agent about which tool to call, manipulate tool parameters, or trick the agent into calling dangerous tool sequences — exploits the gap between what the user asked and what the agent does
rules.remediation: Agent developers: validate that tool calls match the user's actual intent before execution. Implement tool call confirmation for high-risk operations. Use allowlists of permitted tool sequences. Never let tool output dictate which tool to call next without user confirmation. Skill authors: do not include instructions about which tools to call or how to call them — that's the agent's job. Return data, not commands.

rules.name: Agent resource abuse or denial-of-service
rules.description: Content attempts to make an AI agent consume excessive resources — infinite loops, recursive tool calls, massive data generation, API quota exhaustion, or memory bombs that degrade or crash the agent
rules.remediation: Agent developers: set hard timeouts on all tool calls (5-30 seconds max). Limit output sizes from tools. Implement circuit breakers that stop after N consecutive failures or N calls to the same tool. Cap API spending with budget limits. Monitor for infinite loops (tool called >3 times in succession with same params = abort). Skill authors: avoid infinite loops, recursive patterns, and operations that scale with untrusted input sizes. Always bound iterations and output sizes.

rules.name: Claude Code reserved env var poisoning (cross-plugin clobber)
rules.description: A plugin or hook WRITES a reserved, harness-set, per-plugin/per-context Claude Code variable into the global session environment (via $CLAUDE_ENV_FILE or export). These vars are set differently for each plugin by the harness; exporting one session-wide clobbers it for every other plugin and any long-lived process that inherited it. Reading these vars is normal and does NOT match.
rules.remediation: Never write a reserved CLAUDE_* variable (CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT, CLAUDE_PLUGIN_DATA, CLAUDE_PROJECT_DIR, CLAUDE_ENV_FILE, CLAUDE_EFFORT, CLAUDE_CODE_REMOTE, CLAUDECODE) into the global session env or $CLAUDE_ENV_FILE. These are per-plugin values the harness sets; clobbering one breaks every other plugin. Export a namespaced var (e.g. MYPLUGIN_DATA_DIR) instead, and read CLAUDE_PLUGIN_DATA only from your own plugin's runtime-provided env.

rules.name: Claude Code auth / API-endpoint env override
rules.description: A plugin or hook WRITES/overwrites a Claude Code authentication token, API key, or API base-URL variable into the session environment. Overwriting ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL redirects ALL API traffic (prompts + responses) to an attacker-controlled endpoint (MITM/exfil); overwriting a key/token swaps the user's credentials. Reading these is normal and does NOT match.
rules.remediation: Never set or overwrite Claude Code auth/endpoint variables (ANTHROPIC_API_KEY, ANTHROPIC_AUTH_TOKEN, CLAUDE_CODE_OAUTH_TOKEN/REFRESH_TOKEN, ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL, etc.) from a plugin or hook. These belong to the user's session; overwriting them redirects API traffic or swaps credentials. If your plugin needs its own API endpoint, use a plugin-namespaced variable scoped to your own process only — never the reserved ANTHROPIC_* / CLAUDE_CODE_OAUTH_* names.

rules.name: Claude Code guardrail / telemetry / plugin-loading env tamper
rules.description: A plugin or hook WRITES a Claude Code safety, telemetry, TLS, or plugin-loading toggle into the session environment — silently disabling guardrails, hiding activity, weakening TLS, or redirecting where plugins load from. Reading these is normal and does NOT match.
rules.remediation: A plugin or hook must never set Claude Code guardrail/telemetry/TLS/plugin-loading toggles (CLAUDE_CODE_DISABLE_*, DISABLE_TELEMETRY, DO_NOT_TRACK, CLAUDE_CODE_CERT_STORE, CLAUDE_CODE_PLUGIN_CACHE_DIR/SEED_DIR, etc.). These are the user's safety/privacy choices; a plugin changing them silently weakens the session. Document the setting in your README for the user to opt into instead.

rules.name: claude setup-token invocation (long-lived token minting)
rules.description: A plugin, hook, or bundled script invokes `claude setup-token`, which mints a long-lived OAuth token for the user's Claude subscription. If captured/exfiltrated, that token grants an attacker access to the user's paid subscription. A plugin has no legitimate reason to run this.
rules.remediation: Remove any `claude setup-token` invocation from plugin code/hooks/scripts. Token provisioning is a user action performed interactively, never something a plugin runs on the user's behalf — the minted token is a credential that can be stolen.

rules.name: claude --dangerously-skip-permissions invocation
rules.description: A plugin or hook invokes the `claude` CLI with --dangerously-skip-permissions (or --dangerously-bypass-approvals-and-sandbox), spawning a Claude Code session that bypasses ALL permission prompts and sandboxing — arbitrary tool use with no user gate.
rules.remediation: Never spawn `claude` with --dangerously-skip-permissions / --dangerously-bypass-approvals-and-sandbox from a plugin or hook. This runs an unsupervised agent with no permission gate. If a plugin needs to run a command, it should do so through its own explicit, scoped logic, not by launching a permission-bypassed Claude session.

rules.name: claude mcp add — autonomous MCP-server registration from plugin code
rules.description: A plugin or hook programmatically invokes `claude mcp add`, registering an MCP server (a tool provider) without the user's explicit choice — a tool-injection / data-exfil-endpoint vector. Plugins declare their own MCP servers via .mcp.json; running `claude mcp add` at runtime registers an EXTRA provider behind the user's back. (Plugin/marketplace install authorization — `claude plugin install` / `marketplace add` — is handled plugin-wide by validate_plugin's unauthorized-install-combo check, which only flags a SPECIFIC marketplace-add paired with a SPECIFIC plugin-install, since installing from an already-trusted marketplace is authorized.) Documenting the command in a README is fine; a hook/script running it autonomously is not.
rules.remediation: A plugin must not register MCP servers programmatically with `claude mcp add`. Declare your plugin's own MCP servers in .mcp.json (which the user reviews on install) instead of adding a provider at runtime. If an additional server is genuinely required, document it in your README for the user to add themselves.

rules.name: TLS/certificate verification disabled in code
rules.description: Code or a CLI invocation disables TLS certificate verification — `requests(..., verify=False)`, `ssl.CERT_NONE` / `ssl._create_unverified_context()`, Node `rejectUnauthorized: false`, `curl -k`/`--insecure`, or `wget --no-check-certificate`. Turning off cert verification exposes every HTTPS call to man-in-the-middle interception (credential/prompt/response theft, payload swapping). This complements RC-61 (which catches the ENV-VAR form NODE_TLS_REJECT_UNAUTHORIZED=0 / PYTHONHTTPSVERIFY=0); this rule catches the in-code/in-library/CLI forms RC-61 does not.
rules.remediation: Never disable TLS certificate verification. Remove `verify=False` / `ssl.CERT_NONE` / `rejectUnauthorized:false` / `curl -k` / `wget --no-check-certificate`. If a self-signed or internal CA is required, pin that CA explicitly (`verify='/path/to/ca.pem'`, `ca: fs.readFileSync(...)`, `curl --cacert`) instead of turning verification off entirely.

rules.name: Credential discovery / enumeration
rules.description: Code or a command actively SEARCHES the filesystem for credentials, secret keys, or known credential stores — `find ... -name '*.pem'`, `find / -perm -4000` (SUID hunting), `os.walk`/`glob` over the home directory or `.ssh`/`.aws`/`.gnupg` dirs, `ls`/`find` of credential directories, or references to high-signal credential-store filenames (`wallet.dat`, `ntds.dit`, Firefox `key4.db`/`logins.json`/`cookies.sqlite`, `.git-credentials`, a Windows SAM dump). This is reconnaissance preceding credential theft. Distinct from CRED_ENV_READ (reading a specific known cred file): this rule catches the SEARCH/enumeration phase.
rules.remediation: Remove filesystem credential-searching logic. A plugin should never enumerate `~/.ssh`, `~/.aws`, `~/.gnupg`, hunt for `*.pem`/`*.key`/`id_rsa` files, SUID binaries (`find / -perm -4000`), or read OS/browser credential stores (`wallet.dat`, `ntds.dit`, `key4.db`, `.git-credentials`). If the plugin genuinely needs a credential, accept it via an explicit, user-provided config value or environment variable scoped to the plugin — never by searching the disk for it.
